bib.title: 12 Multilevel Models (Statistical Rethinking, first edition, ch. 12)
bib.venue: book chapter, Statistical Rethinking (CRC Press), pp. 355-386

question: How should repeated or clustered observations be modelled so that information is shared across clusters without forgetting (complete pooling) or ignoring (no pooling) it?
hypothesis: Varying intercepts with an adaptively learned prior give better cluster estimates than fixed per-cluster intercepts, because they trade off underfitting and overfitting.
contributions: Introduces varying intercepts, hyperparameters and adaptive regularisation on the reed frog tadpole data
Simulation showing partial pooling beats no pooling, most for small clusters
Cross-classified model (actor and block) on chimpanzee data
Posterior prediction for same clusters, new clusters, and over-dispersion

results.claim: The multilevel tadpole model m12.2 has about 38 effective parameters against 50 actual ones.
results.setup: Reed frog tadpole data (data(reedfrogs)), 48 tanks, binomial survival, fit with map2stan (Stan HMC); m12.2 iter=4000 chains=4
results.table: Table 12.4 compare output, row m12.2, column pWAIC

results.claim: WAIC of multilevel m12.2 beats the fixed-intercept m12.1 by 13.1.
results.setup: Reed frog tadpole data (data(reedfrogs)), 48 tanks, binomial survival, fit with map2stan (Stan HMC)

results.claim: The estimated sd among tanks, sigma, is about 1.6, so the learned prior is fairly strong.
results.setup: Reed frog tadpole data (data(reedfrogs)), 48 tanks, binomial survival, fit with map2stan (Stan HMC)
results.quote: Check the mean of sigma with precis or coef and you’ll see it’s around 1.6.

results.claim: Multilevel model has 12 fewer effective than actual parameters because the prior shrinks intercepts to alpha.
results.setup: Reed frog tadpole data (data(reedfrogs)), 48 tanks, binomial survival, fit with map2stan (Stan HMC)
results.quote: There are 12 fewer effective parameters than actual parameters

results.claim: Estimated population median survival in the tank population is about 0.8, not the empirical mean.
results.setup: Reed frog tadpole data (data(reedfrogs)), 48 tanks, binomial survival, fit with map2stan (Stan HMC); Fig 12.1
results.quote: The horizontal dashed line at about 0.8 is the estimated median survival proportion in the population

results.claim: Shrinkage is stronger for small tanks and for tanks whose empirical proportion lies farther from the global mean; in every tank the multilevel estimate is closer to the mean than the raw proportion.
results.setup: Reed frog tadpole data (data(reedfrogs)), 48 tanks, binomial survival, fit with map2stan (Stan HMC); tank sizes 10, 25, 35 tadpoles (Fig 12.1)
results.quote: Varying intercepts for the smaller tanks, with smaller sample sizes, shrink more.

results.claim: Partial pooling beats no pooling on average in every pond-size group; the gap grows as ponds get smaller (Fig 12.3, read qualitatively, no numeric error values given).
results.setup: Simulated ponds: alpha=1.4, sigma=1.5, 60 ponds, 15 each with n=5,10,25,35, one chain iter=1e4 warmup=1000 (m12.3), error = abs(estimate - true probability)
results.quote: the partial pooling estimates are better on average, especially in smaller ponds.

results.claim: No-pooling errors can exceed 20% in some small ponds.
results.setup: Simulated ponds: alpha=1.4, sigma=1.5, 60 ponds, 15 each with n=5,10,25,35, one chain iter=1e4 warmup=1000 (m12.3), error = abs(estimate - true probability)
results.quote: more than 20% off in some cases

results.claim: Posterior of m12.3 recovers sigma at 1.59 (sd 0.22) against the true 1.5, and a at 1.13 (sd 0.23) against the true 1.4.
results.setup: Simulated ponds: alpha=1.4, sigma=1.5, 60 ponds, 15 each with n=5,10,25,35, one chain iter=1e4 warmup=1000 (m12.3), error = abs(estimate - true probability); one simulated data set
results.table: precis(m12.3), row sigma, column Mean; row a, column Mean 1.13
results.note: The true alpha is 1.4; the estimate is about 1.2 sd below it in this one draw. Chapter does not comment.

results.claim: Exceptions exist: no-pooling can win for ponds with extreme survival probabilities, because few ponds are that extreme.
results.setup: Simulated ponds: alpha=1.4, sigma=1.5, 60 ponds, 15 each with n=5,10,25,35, one chain iter=1e4 warmup=1000 (m12.3), error = abs(estimate - true probability)
results.quote: But sometimes outliers really are outliers.

results.claim: Adding block varying intercepts (m12.5) adds 7 parameters but only about 2.5 effective parameters (pWAIC 10.5 vs 8.1).

results.claim: HMC can handle tens of thousands of varying effect parameters, slowly.

results.claim: Exponential(1) prior is advised over half-Cauchy for variance components when there are few clusters (e.g. 5) or floor/ceiling effects.
results.setup: Overthinking box
results.quote: if you only have 5 clusters, then that’s something like trying to estimate a variance with 5 data points

limits: Frequentist-free but software-specific: all code uses rethinking 1st edition map2stan, which has been superseded (ulam in later editions).
Simulation uses one parameter setting (alpha=1.4, sigma=1.5, 60 ponds) and a single draw; Fig 12.3 gives no numeric errors.
Divergent iterations are flagged and deferred to chapter 13 (non-centred parameterisation).
Half-Cauchy sigma priors may be problematic with few clusters or floor/ceiling effects; the author suggests Exponential(1).
MAP/quadratic approximation cannot fit multilevel models; needs MCMC.
Gaussian population of varying effects is a convention/entropy choice; practice 12M3 explores Cauchy.
practices: Make multilevel regression the default; start multilevel and drop it if unnecessary (p356).
Learn the prior for cluster intercepts from the data: alpha_cluster ~ Normal(alpha, sigma) with hyperpriors (p358-359).
Fit multilevel models with MCMC (map2stan), not map (p359, Overthinking p360).
Use Exponential(1) instead of half-Cauchy for sigma when few clusters or ceiling/floor effects (p363-364).
Simulate data from the model with known parameters to check recovery and to compare estimators (p365-368).
Use as.integer for binomial size variables passed to Stan (p366-367).
Put the grand mean in the linear model and give varying intercepts mean zero; one mean per linear model only (p371-373).
Give each cluster type its own sigma; use sigma as a crude measure of cluster relevance (p373, 376).
Do not expect posterior predictions to match raw data after shrinkage (p376-377).
For new clusters, simulate intercepts from Normal(0, sigma) per posterior sample; show both average-actor and marginal predictions (p378-381).
When two models have near-identical WAIC with dSE larger than the difference, retain and report both (p376).
Use a varying intercept per observation to handle over-dispersion in Poisson/binomial models (p363, 382).
Check multiple chains, n_eff and Rhat (p372, 374).

terms.definition: models forget everything about previous clusters as they move between them; the parameters are independent
the simplest kind of varying effects: a unique intercept per cluster with an adaptively learned common prior
parameters for parameters; their priors are hyperpriors
assumes the population of clusters is invariant: one common intercept; equivalent to zero variation among clusters
each cluster tells nothing about any other; equivalent to assuming infinite variation among clusters
an adaptive regularizing prior producing estimates less underfit than the grand mean and less overfit than no pooling
estimates pulled towards the population mean as a result of regularization
clusters not nested (actors not nested within blocks); hierarchical when nested; specification is typically the same
which level of the model a parameter makes direct predictions for
predictions that average over uncertainty among actors

code.snippet:
m12.2 <- map2stan(
 alist(
 surv ~ dbinom( density , p ) ,
 logit(p) <- a_tank[tank] ,
 a_tank[tank] ~ dnorm( a , sigma ) ,
 a ~ dnorm(0,1) ,
 sigma ~ dcauchy(0,1)
 ), data=d , iter=4000 , chains=4 )
sigma ~ Exponential(1)  (dexp(1) in R code) in place of HalfCauchy(0,1)

a_pond <- rnorm( nponds , mean=a , sd=sigma )
dsim$si <- rbinom( nponds , prob=logistic(dsim$true_a) , size=dsim$ni )

logit(p) <- a + a_actor[actor] + a_block[block_id] + (bp + bpc*condition)*prosoc_left,
a_actor[actor] ~ dnorm( 0 , sigma_actor ),
a_block[block_id] ~ dnorm( 0 , sigma_block ),

a_actor_sims <- rnorm(7000,0,post$sigma_actor)
a_actor_sims <- matrix(a_actor_sims,1000,7)
link.m12.4 <- link( m12.4 , n=1000 , data=d.pred , replace=list(a_actor=a_actor_sims) )

log(mu) <- a + a_society[society] + bp*logpop,
a_society[society] ~ dnorm(0,sigma_society),
